title: Per-request adaptive kernel allocator with lightweight hardware probing
creator: Ethan Kim
description:
Problem: Our current kernel selection is largely offline and coarse-grained (by model + bucketed seq-len). This misses per-request heterogeneity: mixed bursts, token-phase differences, and subtle hardware variability (chiplet placement, transient temperature throttling) that change which kernel is best for a given request. The result: avoidable latency tail and higher per-token cost for a subset of traffic.

Goal: Implement a lightweight, per-request adaptive kernel allocator that probes a tiny microbenchmark when a new execution fingerprint is observed and uses a fast bandit/exp3-style learner plus a warmstart cache to pick kernels for prefill and decode phases separately. The allocator must be safe (no request-visible regressions), inexpensive (<0.5ms median extra overhead per novel fingerprint), and auditable (telemetry + rollback).

Design summary:
- Fingerprint: small deterministic tuple (model, model-shape, nominal-seq-len, device-topology-hash, token-phase-bucket) computed at request admission.
- Probe: at most N=2 tiny microbench runs (prefill matmul and decode attention tile) using very small synthetic inputs timed in a tight loop on the target device/kernel to estimate relative throughput and tail latency. Probes use accel-isolated priority and timebox to 12ms total.
- Bandit learner: contextual bandit (exp3 or Thompson sampling) tracking reward = -latency_cost - alpha*variability where latency_cost is 99th-quantile estimate from probe/memory and variability penalizes high tail. The learner uses priors seeded from offline microbenchmarks for common fingerprints.
- Warmstart cache: cache kernel-choice per-fingerprint with TTL and decay; cache entries record last-choice, success-rate, and telemetry buckets.
- Prefill vs Decode: maintain separate candidate sets and exploration schedules for prefill (latency-sensitive, often long matmuls) and decode (many short attention ops). Kernel candidates include arch-optimized kernels, quantized variants, and fallback generic kernels.
- Safety: if any probe or recent telemetry indicates SLO degradation for the tenant (>p95 threshold configured by route), revert to pinned safe kernel and trigger alert.
- Telemetry: augment request traces with chosen-kernel, probe-metrics, and decision-reason tag. Expose a per-fingerprint dashboard for rollout and drift detection.

Engineering constraints/assumptions:
- Must not require model recompilation in fast path. Probing runs should reuse compiled kernels already present on the node.
- Memory and compute overhead limited: probes scheduled with low priority and timeboxed; avoid cross-tenant noisy probing.
- Works across heterogeneous GPUs (A100, H100, L4); device-topology-hash created from the node discovery layer.

Trade-offs considered:
- More probes increase confidence but add cost and latency risk; chosen default N=2 minimizes extra work while giving a signal.
- Full offline autotuning (heavy microbench corpus) yields better priors but is slow to adapt to transient hardware changes; per-request probing complements offline priors.
- Simpler heuristic (lookup by seq-len bucket) is cheap but brittle for mixed workloads; bandit adapts online but needs good priors and decay controls to limit oscillation.
acceptance_criteria: Per-fingerprint probe overhead median < 0.5ms and 95th < 12ms for cold-new fingerprints (measured on staging cluster).
Average latency tail reduction >= 5% on diversified traffic replay compared to baseline kernel lookup for top 3 customer traffic patterns.
No regressions on pinned-benchmark suite (prefill p99 and decode p99 SLOs) — automated canary gates implemented.
Telemetry emits chosen-kernel, probe timings, and decision-reason for every request; dashboards available in Datadog/Tempo.
Fallback and rollback path exercised in canary for at least 2 customers; automated alerting on >2% route-level SLO delta.
Documentation and runbook for ops: how to interpret fingerprint dashboard and manually pin kernels per route.

progress_updates: 2025-01-18: Proposal created by Ethan. Design review requested with runtime and SRE teams.
2025-01-22: Architecture sync — agreed on fingerprint schema and probe budget (2 runs, 12ms cap). Action: Priya to prototype microprobe harness.
2025-01-28: Prototype microbench implemented in sandbox docker image; initial probe overhead median 0.42ms on H100, 0.55ms on A100. Observed occasional 95th spikes due to node contention.
2025-01-30: Bandit shim POC wired into runtime but disabled behind feature flag. Seed priors loaded from offline microbench corpus (s3://redwood-runtime-bench/prior-v1).
2025-02-02: Canary plan drafted, targeting 2 internal services ~5% of traffic. PR opened: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/12345. Need SRE signoff for probe scheduling policy.
risks: Probe interference: if probes run on busy nodes they may give misleading signals; mitigated by priority isolation, timebox, and retry logic.
Oscillation: aggressive exploration can flip kernels and create micro-flapping; mitigate with decay, momentum term, and sticky TTL.
Security/tenant isolation: probes must never access tenant data; microbench uses synthetic inputs and runs in same process but with strict memory fences.
Operational complexity: large number of fingerprints may create noisy dashboards; provide percentile rollups and automatic pruning.
notes: Design review feedback (2025-01-23): prefer conservative defaults for customer routes with strict SLAs; expose a per-route opt-out flag.
SRE asked to provide per-node probe-capacity metric to avoid overloading small clusters.
Performance team suggests adding a short warmup sample for GPUs with known cold-compilation variance (L4).
Plan to include an A/B evaluation harness that can replay real traffic with kernel-choice overrides to estimate cost delta.
